overview:
It began as a country retreat rather than a town. Around 1229 or 1230, Floris IV, count of Holland, acquired a courtyard and land beside a pond in the dunes near the North Sea — the water survives as the Hofvijver — intending a hunting residence within a wooded enclosure. Floris died before much was built, and it was his son William II, elected king of the Romans, who turned the site into what a contemporary document called a royal palace. William's own son Floris V completed the great hall that still stands as the Ridderzaal, finished around 1290. The settlement that grew up around this complex appears in writing as Die Haghe in 1242; the later form 's-Gravenhage, the count's hedge or enclosure, records exactly what it had been. By the middle of the fourteenth century the counts were living there when in Holland, and the Binnenhof had become the administrative heart of the county.

The oddity that shaped everything afterward is that the place never received city rights. Because it was the count's own seat, the surrounding jurisdiction of the Haagambacht stayed under direct comital administration, and The Hague grew to urban size without walls, without a charter, and without the guild-based self-government that defined Delft, Leiden or Dordrecht. That left it defenseless during the Eighty Years' War against Spain, when it was occupied and largely abandoned in the 1570s, but it also left it politically neutral among Holland's jealous chartered cities — which is part of why the States General of the Dutch Republic settled there permanently in the late sixteenth century. For two centuries the government of one of Europe's richest states, and the diplomatic traffic that came with it, ran out of a place that was technically a village; the Dutch still enjoy calling it the largest village in Europe. City rights arrived only in 1806, from Louis Bonaparte, during the brief Kingdom of Holland.

The nineteenth-century peace movement gave the town a second identity. The Russian tsar's initiative brought twenty-six states to The Hague in 1899 for a conference on disarmament and arbitration, which produced the Permanent Court of Arbitration; a second, larger conference followed in 1907. Andrew Carnegie paid for a building to house the court and a library of international law, its foundation stone laid during the 1907 conference and its doors opened on 28 August 1913, a year before the war those conferences had hoped to forestall. The Peace Palace nonetheless became the address of the World Court and then of the United Nations' International Court of Justice, and the city later accumulated the tribunals for the former Yugoslavia, the International Criminal Court, Europol and Eurojust.
significance: Two things came out of a hunting lodge in the dunes. One is a durable European anomaly: a capital of government that was never a chartered city, whose lack of civic independence made it acceptable to rival cities as a neutral meeting ground, and which has housed the Dutch parliament in a medieval count's courtyard for more than four centuries. The other is the phrase "The Hague" as shorthand for international justice — a usage that begins with the 1899 conference and the Permanent Court of Arbitration, hardens with the Peace Palace and the World Court, and now attaches to the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court. When a head of state is said to be facing The Hague, the reference runs back through Carnegie's donation to a Russian tsar's circular letter, and past that to the reason the town could host such things at all.
coverage: Written from Wikipedia, the Wikidata record, and the Peace Palace's own institutional history; Britannica is cited as background. The dataset holds no events beneath this story, and its 1201 span is a coarse rendering of Wikidata's vague "13th century" inception rather than a real date — the founding is conventionally placed around 1229–1230, with the first documentary mention of Die Haghe in 1242. The comital origins rest on a thin charter record, and the exact date and terms of Floris IV's purchase are reconstructed rather than directly attested; the modern international-institution history and the twentieth-century city itself are barely touched here.
